props.title: Force of Evil
props.initialSlug: Wall Street lawyer corrupted by numbers racket

sections.content: Force of Evil (1948) stands as one of film noir's most scathing indictments of American capitalism, following lawyer Joe Morse's descent into corruption through the numbers racket. Director Abraham Polonsky crafts a searing critique that influenced later crime films like The Godfather (1972) and Wall Street (1987). The film's poetic dialogue and expressionistic cinematography by George Barnes elevate it beyond typical noir, creating a haunting meditation on moral corruption that feels startlingly modern.

sections.content: The film's influence on later crime cinema cannot be overstated. Martin Scorsese frequently cites Force of Evil as a major inspiration, particularly for Mean Streets (1973) and Goodfellas (1990). The way Polonsky frames capitalism as inherently corrupt, with Joe Morse's attempts to "legitimize" illegal gambling serving as a metaphor for Wall Street practices, resonates through films like The Big Short (2015) and Margin Call (2011).

Visually, cinematographer George Barnes creates a noir landscape that pushes beyond genre conventions. His use of deep shadows and canted angles influenced later neo-noir classics like Chinatown (1974) and Night Moves (1975). The film's revolutionary approach to urban spaces, treating New York's financial district as a concrete jungle where moral compromise festers, set a template for how cinema depicts corporate corruption. sections.content: Polonsky's communist sympathies and eventual blacklisting add another layer to Force of Evil. The film's critique of capitalism made it a target during the Red Scare, yet its themes resonate through politically charged noirs like On the Waterfront (1954) and modern films like Michael Clayton (2007). The way it portrays financial systems as inherently corrupt influenced generations of filmmakers tackling white-collar crime.
